question: When sparse-parity training appears stuck before an abrupt phase transition, is SGD performing memoryless search or accumulating a measurable internal signal near the statistical-query computational frontier?

key_findings.claim: Sparse parity is an intentionally severe feature-learning test because incorrect subsets provide no correlation feedback under the uniform input distribution.
key_findings.evidence: Distinct parity functions are orthogonal, producing an SQ tradeoff T/tau-squared at least on the order of n-to-the-k for constant-noise queries, while the statistical sample limit is only about k log n. The paper also notes that noiseless parity is solvable by Gaussian elimination, so the SQ bound is not a universal computational lower bound.

anchors.section: Appendix A.1, parity and SQ background

key_findings.claim: A broad but small-instance sweep finds that standard gradient-based training can learn sparse parities without an explicit sparse initialization prior.
key_findings.evidence: For n in 10, 20, 30 and k in 2, 3, 4, the authors sweep 15 architecture configurations, batch sizes 1-1024, three initializations, three losses, and four learning rates. Every configuration has at least one learning rate attaining 100 percent test-batch accuracy in at least 20 percent of 25 trials within 100,000 steps; minimal-width MLPs and the Transformer require batch size at least 16 for the stated robustness.

anchors.section: Section 3.1, Robust Space of Positive Results

key_findings.claim: Convergence-time evidence conflicts with a simple memoryless random-search account.
key_findings.evidence: Success times lack the early lucky mass expected from geometric random search, runs sharing initialization but changing minibatches are strongly correlated, convergence adapts to sparsity k, width gives diminishing rather than linear parallel speedup, and scaling curves develop elbows at larger n.

anchors.section: Section 3.2, Random Search or Hidden Progress?
Appendix C.3-C.4, hidden progress and width

key_findings.claim: A Fourier gap in the population gradient explains how relevant parity coordinates can emerge before loss improves.
key_findings.evidence: For a ReLU neuron at all-ones initialization, relevant coordinates expose degree-(k-1) Fourier coefficients of majority while irrelevant coordinates expose degree-(k+1) coefficients. Their gap is on the order of n to minus (k-1)/2, permitting recovery from roughly n-to-(k-1) samples up to logarithms.

key_findings.claim: The end-to-end MLP theorem is substantially narrower and more resource-intensive than the empirical claim.
key_findings.evidence: Theorem 4 covers even k, odd sufficiently large n, a specially constructed symmetric sign-vector initialization, hinge loss, width exponential in k, and batch size on the order of n-to-k times logs. The authors explicitly state that it does not cover Gaussian/uniform initialization or the observed batch-size-one success.

key_findings.claim: Low-width success requires learned features rather than a fixed low-dimensional kernel representation.
key_findings.evidence: Theorem 5 states that any bounded D-dimensional embedding with insufficient D times norm budget fails on at least one k-parity. Thus the low-width trained networks lie outside a fixed-feature/NTK explanation, although the paper acknowledges better sample bounds in a much larger NTK regime.

anchors.section: Theorem 5, Low-Width NTK Cannot Fit All Parities

key_findings.claim: An idealized disjoint-PolyNet proves that a long accuracy plateau can conceal deterministic cumulative progress.
key_findings.evidence: The model assumes the input is partitioned into k blocks with exactly one relevant variable per block. Theorem 6 shows gradient flow spends a 1-o(1) fraction of convergence time above 49 percent error, and Theorem 7 gives high-probability online-SGD convergence with an adaptive schedule in roughly (n/k)^(2k-1) log(1/epsilon) steps.

key_findings.claim: White-box measures reveal gradual change even when black-box loss and accuracy are flat.
key_findings.evidence: Population-gradient Fourier gaps and the infinity norm of movement from initialization increase before the accuracy transition. In finite-data runs with weight decay, training error reaches zero well before test error, producing grokking; a deeper polynomial network also supplies a counterexample to greedy layer-wise learning.

method.core_idea: Use sparse parity as a controlled computational-statistical gap and inspect both scaling behavior and internal Fourier-aligned state to distinguish hidden feature amplification from blind search.
method.mechanism: Empirically sweep MLPs, one-neuron oscillatory models, Transformers, and polynomial networks over size, batch, initialization, loss, and learning rate. Theoretically identify parity coordinates in population gradients through a degree-(k-1) versus degree-(k+1) Fourier gap, lift a special case to an MLP convergence theorem, rule out low-dimensional fixed features, and derive exact gradient-flow/SGD dynamics for a partition-aware product network.
assumptions: Inputs are uniformly random Boolean vectors and labels are a noiseless k-sparse parity except in dedicated noise experiments.
The main empirical runtime claim selects the best of four learning rates and accepts at least 20-percent success across 25 trials.
The MLP theorem uses a purpose-built symmetric sign initialization, even k, hinge loss, very large batches, and width exponential in k.
The disjoint-PolyNet is given a partition containing exactly one relevant coordinate in every block.
Online training receives fresh independent samples each iteration, coupling runtime and data consumption.

techniques.role: Separates statistical sample sufficiency from SQ-like gradient computation and exposes sparsity-dependent scaling.
Ranks gradient coordinates by the separation between relevant lower-degree and irrelevant higher-degree Fourier coefficients.
Tests whether convergence is driven more by persistent initialized state than by minibatch luck.
Rules out a small fixed kernel representation as an explanation for learning all target parities.
Makes hidden feature amplification and a plateau-to-transition trajectory analytically tractable.
Tracks Fourier gaps and infinity-norm weight movement before black-box metrics change.

evaluations.setting: Noiseless sparse parity for n up to 30 and k up to 4 across 15 neural configurations.
evaluations.metric: Steps to 100-percent accuracy on a fixed 8192-example validation batch, success probability across 25 trials, and coarse power-law fits.
evaluations.result: Every swept configuration succeeds in at least 20 percent of trials for some learning rate within 100,000 steps; some minimal and Transformer settings need batch size at least 16.
evaluations.baseline: Multiple architectures, batch sizes, losses, initializations, and learning rates rather than one conventional baseline.

evaluations.setting: Repeated stochastic training from shared versus independent initializations.
evaluations.metric: Correlation and dispersion of convergence times and loss curves.
evaluations.result: Runs sharing initialization are much more similar than the memoryless random-search hypothesis predicts.
evaluations.baseline: Independent initialization and a geometric-time exhaustive-search model.

evaluations.setting: Width scaling on fixed sparse-parity instances.
evaluations.result: Speedups diminish and eventually plateau, except at extremely large widths where parallel search can reappear.
evaluations.baseline: Ideal 1/r parallel speedup from r independent random searches.

evaluations.setting: Finite training sets for a width-100 ReLU MLP with minibatch SGD and weight decay.
evaluations.metric: Time to zero training versus zero test error across sample sizes.
evaluations.result: Smaller samples show delayed generalization after memorization, reproducing grokking on sparse parity.
evaluations.baseline: Larger finite samples and the online fresh-sample regime.

evaluations.setting: Disjoint-PolyNet under gradient flow and online SGD.
evaluations.metric: Fraction of convergence time spent above 49-percent error and steps to epsilon error.
evaluations.result: Analysis proves a long plateau followed by a rapid transition and n-to-O(k) convergence under the partition-aware model.
evaluations.baseline: A memoryless search interpretation and black-box loss alone.

limitations: The task is a heavily idealized synthetic Boolean problem, and transfer to natural-language, program-synthesis, or real combinatorial tasks is untested.
The robust empirical grid uses only n at most 30 and k at most 4; several illustrative n=50 experiments do not establish asymptotic scaling.
Selecting the best learning rate and requiring only 20-percent success makes the headline universality weaker than a default-training guarantee.
Power-law fits develop elbows as n grows, so reported near-limit scaling on small instances should not be extrapolated freely.
The central MLP theorem does not cover ordinary random initialization, small batches, odd k, Transformers, or most empirical losses.
Online SGD uses a new batch every step, conflating computational time with independent sample count.
The exact disjoint-PolyNet theory assumes useful prior knowledge about the partition of candidate variables.
The SQ lower bound does not constrain algorithms such as Gaussian elimination that consume exact noiseless examples.
failure_modes: A flat loss curve can coexist with feature progress, but can also be genuine stagnation; the proposed measures require white-box access and task-specific Fourier structure.
At larger dimensions the empirical exponent worsens, invalidating a naive small-n scaling fit.
Small-batch gradient noise can obscure the Fourier coordinate gap even when population gradients are informative.
Sign-vector initialization and parity symmetry may create a mechanism absent in ordinary continuous initializations or real data.
A model may memorize a finite parity sample without discovering the true subset, delaying or preventing generalization.
Very large width can shift the mechanism toward parallel lottery search, so one explanation need not hold across scaling regimes.
Label noise weakens correlations and makes success unstable at small batch sizes.
reusable_insights: Audit apparent phase transitions with internal progress measures before concluding that learning began abruptly.
Condition repeated runs on initialization to separate persistent feature luck from fresh stochastic-batch luck.
Scale data, iterations, width, and retry probability independently; a single aggregate compute axis can hide a resource tradeoff.
State clearly whether a lower bound applies to noisy statistical queries, exact examples, or all algorithms.
Use matched low-width lower bounds to determine whether observed success genuinely requires feature learning.
Treat small-instance power laws as hypotheses and search explicitly for elbows before extrapolation.
Report the learning-rate search and per-seed success distribution, not only the best converged curve.
open_questions: Can the Fourier-gap convergence argument cover Gaussian initialization, odd k, small batches, and common losses?
What task-agnostic progress measure predicts eventual emergence on real combinatorial or language tasks?
How do sample size, iteration count, width, and restart budget trade off when controlled independently at larger n and k?
Where exactly does the mechanism transition from sequential feature amplification to width-driven parallel search?
Can one predict failure or convergence time from initialization before expensive training?
Do comparable hidden signals exist in Transformers on parity without relying on an MLP-style Fourier derivation?

competitive_landscape.title: Learning Parities with Neural Networks
competitive_landscape.relationship: A direct precursor proving that depth-two gradient descent can learn sparse parities under specially structured distributions.
competitive_landscape.difference: Daniely and Malach alter the distribution to expose learnable structure; Hidden Progress focuses on uniform noiseless inputs, a broader architecture sweep, resource scaling, and the internal Fourier-gap trajectory.

competitive_landscape.title: An initial alignment between neural network and target is needed for gradient descent to learn
competitive_landscape.relationship: A complementary lower-bound account of when noisy gradient descent can learn Boolean targets.
competitive_landscape.difference: Abbe et al. formalize initial alignment as a necessary condition under symmetric i.i.d. initialization; Hidden Progress supplies a positive parity mechanism where a small Fourier alignment is present and subsequently amplified.

competitive_landscape.title: Matching the Statistical Query Lower Bound for k-Sparse Parity Problems with Sign Stochastic Gradient Descent
competitive_landscape.relationship: A later result targeting the same sparse-parity computational frontier with a sharper gradient-based algorithm.
competitive_landscape.difference: Kou et al. analyze sign SGD and obtain approximately d^(k-1) samples with 2^Theta(k) neurons for k up to order sqrt(d), explicitly claiming a match to the SQ frontier; Hidden Progress uses ordinary SGD-style dynamics, offers broader empirical phenomena, but has more restrictive and looser theory.

competitive_landscape.title: Pareto Frontiers in Deep Feature Learning: Data, Compute, Width, and Luck
competitive_landscape.relationship: A direct follow-up that turns the sparse-parity SQ lower bound into an explicit multi-resource tradeoff frontier.
competitive_landscape.difference: Edelman et al. separate offline dataset size, width, iterations, and retry luck and show sparse initialization plus width can improve sample efficiency, extending the resource questions that Hidden Progress only begins to probe in online training.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: The paper claims that standard neural training solves small sparse-parity instances near the sparsity-dependent SQ limit through gradual Fourier-aligned feature amplification hidden beneath abrupt loss transitions.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: The combination of broad empirical stress testing, initialization-conditioned diagnostics, a concrete Fourier progress signal, and an exact phase-transition model is genuinely illuminating. The phrase near the computational limit needs careful qualification: the SQ bound is model-specific, the main MLP theorem requires enormous batches and special initialization, and later sign-SGD work provides a sharper match.

reviewer_notes: Read the complete 52-page extraction, including the empirical grid, random-search audits, Fourier derivation, MLP and fixed-feature theorems, disjoint-PolyNet analysis, finite-data grokking/noise/depth appendices, architecture definitions, and scaling protocol. Primary arXiv/OpenReview records for four direct predecessors or successors were checked on 2026-08-23.
